blocks.text: Practice short questions for the whole of Chapter 13 (Thermal Physics), arranged by the chapter's sections, in the style of a 2-mark Board short question. Each answer is a short model answer; small numericals show the working, and a comparison is answered as a table.

blocks.prompt: 1 What is thermal physics? Which two areas of knowledge does it need?
blocks.explanation: Thermal physics deals with the relationship between heat, work, temperature and other forms of energy. Its study needs the knowledge of statistical mechanics and the kinetic theory of gases.

book_ref.quote: Thermal physics is an important area of study

blocks.prompt: 2 Differentiate between a macroscopic system and a microscopic system.
blocks.explanation: A macroscopic system has many atoms or molecules; a microscopic system has a single atom or molecule.

book_ref.quote: Macroscopic systems have properties such as temperature and pressure

rows: A large system containing many atoms or molecules.
A system consisting of a single atom or molecule.
Properties: temperature and pressure (thermal properties of the whole system).
Can be studied without reference to the molecular nature of matter.
Deals with an individual atom or molecule.

blocks.prompt: 3 Name four daily-life applications of the kinetic theory of gases.
blocks.explanation: Automobile engines, turbines, pumps and air conditioners (also production of food and the environment).

book_ref.quote: There are number of applications of the kinetic theory of gases in daily life

blocks.prompt: 4 Define Brownian motion.
blocks.explanation: Brownian motion is the random (zig-zag) motion of small particles suspended in a fluid, such as pollen particles in water, caused by collisions with the fluid's molecules.

book_ref.quote: Brownian motion is the random motion of small particles suspended in a fluid

blocks.prompt: 5 What did Robert Brown observe, and when?
blocks.explanation: In 1827 the botanist Robert Brown observed under a microscope that tiny pollen particles in a liquid were moving around randomly. This was later proved to be an effect of molecular motion.

book_ref.quote: Robert Brown, a botanist observed under microscope

blocks.prompt: 6 Why does a gas molecule follow a zig-zag path?
blocks.explanation: A molecule changes its path after every collision with another molecule. Since it keeps on colliding, and each collision exchanges momentum and energy, its path becomes random or zig-zag.

book_ref.quote: A molecule in a gas changes its path after collision with another molecule.

blocks.prompt: 7 How does the mass (size) of particles affect the speed of Brownian motion?
blocks.explanation: The transfer of momentum is inversely proportional to the mass of the particles, so lighter (smaller) particles obtain greater speeds from collisions and move faster.

book_ref.quote: We know that the transfer of momentum is inversely proportional to the mass of the particles.

blocks.prompt: 8 What is viscosity? How does it affect Brownian motion?
blocks.explanation: Viscosity is the magnitude of internal friction in a fluid, i.e. its resistance to flow. The speed of the particles is inversely proportional to viscosity, so low viscosity gives faster Brownian movement.

book_ref.quote: The speed of the particles is inversely proportional to the viscosity of the fluid.

blocks.prompt: 9 Who explained Brownian motion and who verified the explanation experimentally?
blocks.explanation: Albert Einstein explained the pollen movement, assisted by molecules, in 1905. The French physicist J Perrin verified it experimentally in 1908 and received the 1926 Nobel Prize in physics.

book_ref.quote: which earned him the 1926 Nobel Prize in physics

blocks.prompt: 10 Why is Brownian motion called a simple model of randomness?
blocks.explanation: Because the particles move in random, irregular directions due to unpredictable molecular collisions; the motion describes randomness and chaos, so it is one of the simple models of randomness.

book_ref.quote: Brownian motion describes randomness and chaos

blocks.prompt: 11 What does the kinetic theory of gases describe? How does gas pressure arise according to it?
blocks.explanation: It describes the molecular composition of a gas and the motion of its molecules. Gas pressure arises because the particles collide with each other and with the walls of the container.

book_ref.quote: The kinetic theory of gases describes the molecular composition of the gas and their motion.

blocks.prompt: 12 State any four basic assumptions of the kinetic theory of gases.
blocks.explanation: (1) A gas consists of a very large number of tiny spherical particles far apart compared to their sizes. (2) The particles are in constant rapid motion in random directions. (3) Collisions between particles and with the walls are perfectly elastic. (4) There are no forces of attraction or repulsion between particles except during collisions; the average K.E. depends on temperature.

book_ref.quote: However, the basic assumptions are:

blocks.prompt: 13 Define mean free path.
blocks.explanation: The mean free path is the average distance a moving particle covers before it undergoes a collision that significantly alters its direction or energy.

book_ref.quote: The mean free path is average distance a moving particle covered

blocks.prompt: 14 Why is the volume of gas particles neglected in the kinetic theory?
blocks.explanation: Gas particles are tiny and far apart compared to their sizes, so the volume of the particles themselves is negligible compared with the volume of the empty spaces between them.

book_ref.quote: Volume of the gas particles is negligible compared to the volume of the empty spaces.

blocks.prompt: 15 Name the transport properties described by the kinetic theory of gases.
blocks.explanation: Viscosity, thermal conductivity and diffusivity. (The theory also defines temperature, volume and pressure.)

book_ref.quote: It also defines properties such as temperature, volume and pressure

blocks.text: 13.3 Pressure in a Gas and Derivation of PV = ⅓Nm<v²>

blocks.prompt: 16 Define the pressure of a gas on the basis of the kinetic theory.
blocks.explanation: When molecules strike the walls they exert force due to the change in momentum in each collision. The pressure of a gas is the force exerted per unit area of the container walls as a result of these collisions.

book_ref.quote: When gas molecules strike the walls, they exert a force on them due to the change in momentum during each collision.

blocks.prompt: 17 Show that the ideal gas law PV = nRT can be written as PV = Nk_BT.
blocks.explanation: Since R = N_Ak_B, PV = nN_Ak_BT. The number of moles is n = N/N_A, so PV = (N/N_A)N_Ak_BT = Nk_BT.

book_ref.quote: where P is the pressure, n is number of moles, R is general gas constant

blocks.prompt: 18 How many molecules are there in 2.0 × 10⁻³ m³ of an ideal gas at 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa and 290 K? (k_B = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹)

book_ref.quote: (N_A = 6.02 × 10²³ molecules) is the Avogadro number

blocks.prompt: 19 Find the change in momentum of a molecule that strikes a wall with velocity vₓ and rebounds elastically.
blocks.explanation: Initial momentum = mvₓ; final momentum = −mvₓ. Δp = −mvₓ − (mvₓ) = −2mvₓ. The magnitude is 2mvₓ.

book_ref.quote: It rebounds elastically in the opposite direction having velocity –v

blocks.prompt: 20 Why is the time between two consecutive collisions of a molecule with the same wall equal to 2L/vₓ?
blocks.explanation: After hitting one wall the molecule travels L to the opposite wall and L back, a distance 2L, with x-speed vₓ. So Δt = distance/speed = 2L/vₓ.

book_ref.quote: It moves back and forth, colliding at regular intervals with the walls

blocks.prompt: 21 A molecule of mass 4.0 × 10⁻²⁶ kg moves with vₓ = 300 m s⁻¹ in a cubical box of side 0.050 m. Find the average force it exerts on one wall.

book_ref.quote: This molecule has mass m, and is moving with speed

blocks.prompt: 22 Why are velocities squared before averaging in the kinetic theory?
blocks.explanation: A molecule strikes a wall with vₓ and leaves with −vₓ, so the simple average velocity is zero. Squaring makes every term positive, so the average <vₓ²> is not zero.

book_ref.quote: This means simple average does not work here.

blocks.prompt: 23 Define root mean square (rms) velocity.
blocks.explanation: The rms velocity is the square root of the average of the squares of the velocities: vᵣₘₛ = √<v²>, where <v²> = (v₁² + v₂² + ... + v_N²)/N.

book_ref.quote: is known as the root mean square (rms) velocity and is written as:

blocks.prompt: 24 Three molecules have speeds 2, 4 and 6 m s⁻¹. Find their average speed and rms speed.

book_ref.quote: In order to avoid this zero, we need to do the square of the velocities before averaging.

blocks.prompt: 25 Why is <vₓ²> = <v²>/3 for a gas?
blocks.explanation: <v²> = <vₓ²> + <v_y²> + <v_z²>. The molecules move randomly with the same average speed in all three directions, so the three terms are equal: <v²> = 3<vₓ²>, i.e. <vₓ²> = <v²>/3.

book_ref.quote: Since gas molecules are moving randomly and have the same average speed in all three directions.

blocks.prompt: 26 Write the pressure of a gas in terms of its density and find the rms speed when P = 2.0 × 10⁵ Pa and ρ = 1.5 kg m⁻³.

book_ref.quote: This is the pressure of the gas molecules on the wall.

blocks.prompt: 27 Starting from PV = ⅓Nm<v²>, show that P = ⅔N₀<K.E._T>.
blocks.explanation: P = (N/3V)m<v²> = ⅔(N/V)<½mv²>. Writing N/V = N₀ (molecules per unit volume) and <½mv²> = <K.E._T> gives P = ⅔N₀<K.E._T>.

book_ref.quote: Rearranging the pressure, Eq. (13.13) for P, and substituting the density

blocks.prompt: 28 A carbon dioxide molecule has a mass of 44 u. Find its mass in kilograms. (1 u = 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg)

book_ref.quote: Mass of oxygen O₂ = 32 × 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg = 5.3 × 10⁻²⁶ kg

blocks.prompt: 29 Find the rms speed of helium atoms of mass 6.64 × 10⁻²⁷ kg at 300 K. (k_B = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹)

book_ref.quote: What is the rms speed of air molecules (O₂ and N₂) at room temperature e.g. 25 °C?

blocks.prompt: 30 How does the rms speed of air molecules at room temperature compare with the speed of sound in air?
blocks.explanation: At 25 °C the rms speeds are about 481 m s⁻¹ (O₂) and 515 m s⁻¹ (N₂), much greater than the speed of sound, which is about 340 m s⁻¹.

book_ref.quote: The speed of air molecules is much greater than the speed of sound which is about 340 m s⁻¹.

blocks.prompt: 31 Explain the popping of popcorn on the basis of the kinetic theory of gases.
blocks.explanation: On heating, the moisture trapped in the kernel becomes steam. The pressure inside the kernel increases until it ruptures the cover, releasing gelatinous starch, which becomes solid after cooling.

book_ref.quote: When popcorn kernel is heated, the moisture trapped in popcorn kernel becomes steam.

blocks.prompt: 32 Why does the pressure inside a car tyre rise when air is pumped into it?
blocks.explanation: Pumping increases the number of air molecules in the limited volume of the tyre, so molecular collisions with the tyre's walls become more frequent and the pressure rises. This pressure gives the tyre its hardness.

book_ref.quote: more molecules result in frequent molecular collisions with tyre's walls due to limited volume

blocks.text: 13.4 Average Translational Kinetic Energy of a Gas

blocks.prompt: 33 What is the Boltzmann constant? Give its value and its relation with R and N_A.
blocks.explanation: The Boltzmann constant is the gas constant per molecule: k_B = R/N_A = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹ (or 8.62 × 10⁻⁵ eV K⁻¹).

book_ref.quote: However, M/m is simply Avogadro's number i.e. N_A = M m⁻¹.

blocks.prompt: 34 Write the expression for the rms speed of gas molecules in terms of R and T, and show how it depends on temperature.
blocks.explanation: Equating nRT = (N/3)mvᵣₘₛ² gives vᵣₘₛ = √(3RT/mN_A), where mN_A is the mass of one mole. So vᵣₘₛ ∝ √T.

book_ref.quote: We have calculated the pressure of the gas molecule

blocks.prompt: 35 Write the relation between the average translational kinetic energy of gas molecules and the absolute temperature. What does it show?
blocks.explanation: <K.E._T> = ½mvᵣₘₛ² = (3/2)k_BT. The average translational K.E. is a constant times T, so the temperature of a gas is a direct measure of the average translational K.E. of its molecules.

book_ref.quote: the temperature of a gas is a direct measure of the average translational kinetic energy of its molecules

blocks.prompt: 36 Find the average translational kinetic energy of a gas molecule at 227 °C. (k_B = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹)

book_ref.quote: is given by a simple constant times the temperature

blocks.prompt: 37 Define the electron volt and give its value in joules.
blocks.explanation: One electron volt is the kinetic energy of an electron accelerated through a voltage difference of one volt. 1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. It is used for very small energies such as k_BT.

book_ref.quote: The electron volt is the kinetic energy of an electron

blocks.prompt: 38 Find the value of k_BT at 1000 K in electron volts. (k_B = 8.62 × 10⁻⁵ eV K⁻¹)

book_ref.quote: so at room temperature, value of k_BT

blocks.prompt: 39 The absolute temperature of a gas is tripled. What happens to (i) the average translational K.E. and (ii) the rms speed of its molecules?
blocks.explanation: (i) <K.E.> = (3/2)k_BT ∝ T, so it becomes 3 times. (ii) vᵣₘₛ ∝ √T, so it becomes √3 = 1.73 times.

book_ref.quote: In this equation, 1/2mv²ₘᵣₛ is the average translational kinetic energy

blocks.prompt: 40 Find the ratio of the rms speeds of the molecules of a gas at 600 K and at 150 K.
blocks.explanation: vᵣₘₛ ∝ √T, so v₆₀₀/v₁₅₀ = √(600/150) = √4 = 2. The ratio is 2 : 1.

book_ref.quote: We rewrite the pressure equation as

blocks.prompt: 41 How does the kinetic theory help in protecting the environment?
blocks.explanation: Kinetic theory helps us understand the interaction between pollutants and the atmosphere. This knowledge is used to develop systems that monitor the quality of air.

book_ref.quote: This knowledge is used to develop the systems to monitor the quality of air.

blocks.prompt: 42 What is statistical physics? Why is it needed for a gas?
blocks.explanation: Statistical physics is the branch of physics that uses probability theory. A gas has a very large number of molecules with different speeds and energy states, so it is described statistically.

book_ref.quote: For large number of molecule, we use statistical physics.

blocks.prompt: 43 State the Boltzmann distribution law and define the Boltzmann factor.
blocks.explanation: N₂/N₁ = e^(−ΔE/k_BT), where N₁, N₂ are the populations of the lower and higher energy states and ΔE = E₂ − E₁. The term e^(−ΔE/k_BT) is the Boltzmann factor.

book_ref.quote: This equation is known as the Boltzmann distribution law and is important

blocks.prompt: 44 Why do more particles reside in lower energy states than in higher ones?
blocks.explanation: The probability of finding molecules in an energy state varies exponentially as −E/k_BT. For a higher state ΔE > 0, so N₂/N₁ = e^(−ΔE/k_BT) < 1; hence more particles are in lower states.

book_ref.quote: It states that the probability of finding the molecules in a particular energy state

blocks.prompt: 45 Two energy levels differ by ΔE = 3k_BT. Find the ratio of the populations N₂/N₁.
blocks.explanation: N₂/N₁ = e^(−ΔE/k_BT) = e^(−3) = 0.050. The higher level has only about 5% of the population of the lower level.

book_ref.quote: Boltzmann constant is also related to the population of atoms in two levels.

blocks.prompt: 46 The speed of a gas molecule changes at every collision. How then can we speak of its average kinetic energy at temperature T?
blocks.explanation: A molecule undergoes billions of collisions every second, each changing its speed and K.E. But averaged over so many collisions, kinetic theory gives a fixed average: E_av = (3/2)k_BT.

book_ref.quote: Each collision changes the speed of molecule thereby changing the kinetic energy

blocks.prompt: 47 What was Maxwell's contribution to the kinetic theory?
blocks.explanation: In 1860 James Clerk Maxwell derived an expression for the distribution of molecular speeds within a system at thermal equilibrium. Experiments confirmed his predictions about 60 years later.

book_ref.quote: In 1860 James Clerk Maxwell (1831–1879) derived an expression

blocks.prompt: 48 What are neutron stars? Why are they difficult to study?
blocks.explanation: Neutron stars are among the densest known objects, second only to black holes; their matter behaves like a degenerate gas. The nearest are many parsecs away, and their strong gravitational fields make them hard to model.

book_ref.quote: Neutron stars are among the densest known objects in the universe

blocks.prompt: 49 What are pulsars? How is their radiation believed to be produced?
blocks.explanation: Pulsars are relatively young, rapidly rotating neutron stars that emit beams of radiation. The radiation is believed to be produced when strong magnetic fields channel matter toward the magnetic poles of the neutron star.

book_ref.quote: Many of the neutron stars observed so far are relatively young and rotate rapidly

blocks.prompt: 50 Why does the magnetic field of a star become very strong when it collapses into a neutron star?
blocks.explanation: During the collapse of the stellar core both mass and field are compressed. The magnetic field lines are squeezed closer together, and closer field lines mean a stronger field.

book_ref.quote: Magnetic fields represented by field lines become stronger

blocks.prompt: 51 How was the Sun formed?
blocks.explanation: About 4.6 billion years ago the Sun formed from a huge cloud of gas and dust (solar nebula). Gravitational contraction raised the central temperature, forming a protostar; when the core became very hot, fusion of hydrogen into helium began.

book_ref.quote: The Sun is the nearest star to Earth and the main source of heat and light for our planet.

blocks.prompt: 52 Name the life stages of the Sun in order. In which stage is it at present?
blocks.explanation: Nebula → protostar → main sequence → red giant → planetary nebula → white dwarf. At present the Sun is in the main sequence stage, converting hydrogen into helium.

book_ref.quote: The life stages of the Sun are

blocks.prompt: 53 Why is the Sun important in thermal physics?
blocks.explanation: The Sun is a natural source of enormous heat energy, produced by nuclear fusion of hydrogen into helium, and it transfers this energy mainly by radiation.

book_ref.quote: In thermal physics, the Sun is important because

blocks.prompt: 54 A star has mass 1.5 × 10³⁰ kg, radius 8 × 10⁸ m and internal pressure 2 × 10¹⁴ Pa. Using P_g ≈ GM²/R⁴, decide whether it will expand or contract. (G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²)
blocks.explanation: P_g = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × (1.5 × 10³⁰)²/(8 × 10⁸)⁴ = 1.50 × 10⁵¹/4.10 × 10³⁵ = 3.7 × 10¹⁴ Pa. This is greater than 2 × 10¹⁴ Pa, so gravity wins and the star contracts.

book_ref.quote: A star has mass 2 × 10³⁰ kg and radius 7 × 10⁸ m.

blocks.prompt: 55 What is stellar evolution? On what does the life of a star depend?
blocks.explanation: Stellar evolution deals with how a star changes over time. Lifetimes range from a few million to trillions of years, and the life of a star depends on its mass.

book_ref.quote: Stellar evolution deals with the star changes over the time.

blocks.prompt: 56 Which stars live longest and which live shortest?
blocks.explanation: The least massive stars (red dwarfs) live longest, up to trillions of years, longer than the present age of the universe. The most massive stars live only a few million years.

book_ref.quote: the most massive stars live only a few million years

blocks.prompt: 57 How does a cloud of gas and dust become a star?
blocks.explanation: A nebula (molecular cloud) contracts; its density and temperature rise because the K.E. of particles rises (K.E. ∝ T), forming a protostar. After millions of years it becomes a star when it reaches equilibrium.

book_ref.quote: After a millions of years, these proto-stars can become a star

blocks.prompt: 58 Write the hydrostatic equation of a star and state what the negative sign shows.
blocks.explanation: ΔP/Δr = −GMᵣρᵣ/r², where Mᵣ is the mass within radius r and ρᵣ the density at r. The negative sign shows that pressure decreases outward while gravity pulls inward.

book_ref.quote: This condition is described by the hydrostatic equation;

blocks.prompt: 59 What is the role of nuclear fusion in the life of a star?
blocks.explanation: When the core temperature rises, hydrogen nuclei fuse to form helium, releasing immense energy. This energy powers the star for most of its life and maintains equilibrium against gravitational collapse.

book_ref.quote: This process releases an immense amount of energy

blocks.prompt: 60 What happens in the red giant stage of a star?
blocks.explanation: With rising temperature and changing core composition the star expands into a red giant. Stars with at least about half the Sun's mass begin helium fusion, producing carbon and oxygen; massive stars continue fusing heavier elements up to iron.

book_ref.quote: the star may expand significantly to become a red giant

blocks.prompt: 61 Differentiate between the end of a low or intermediate mass star and that of a star about ten times the Sun's mass.
blocks.explanation: Low and intermediate mass stars end quietly as white dwarfs; very massive stars end in a supernova.

book_ref.quote: In low and intermediate mass stars

header: Star about ten times the Sun's mass
rows: Core contracts into a dense white dwarf.
Outer layers are expelled into space as a planetary nebula.
The inert iron core collapses under gravity.
Remnant: neutron star or black hole.

blocks.prompt: 62 Why has no red dwarf yet completed its life cycle, and what will it finally become?
blocks.explanation: Red dwarfs have low mass and use fuel very efficiently, so they evolve very slowly; the universe is not yet old enough for any to finish. Models say they will become hotter and brighter, then evolve into low mass white dwarfs.

book_ref.quote: Red dwarf stars, due to their low mass and highly efficient fuel consumption

blocks.prompt: 63 What is a parsec? Express 10 parsec in kilometres.
blocks.explanation: A parsec is a unit of distance used by astronomers; 1 parsec ≈ 3.26 light years ≈ 31 trillion km (3.1 × 10¹³ km). So 10 parsec ≈ 3.1 × 10¹⁴ km.

book_ref.quote: A parsec is a unit of distance that is used by astronomers

blocks.prompt: 64 Differentiate between a white dwarf and a neutron star.
blocks.explanation: A white dwarf is the dense core left by a low or intermediate mass star; a neutron star is left after the supernova of a much more massive star.

book_ref.quote: leading to the formation of dense remnants such as neutron stars or black holes

rows: Formed when the core of a low or intermediate mass star contracts.
Formed when the iron core of a star about ten times the Sun's mass collapses in a supernova.
Outer layers form a planetary nebula.
Final stage of the Sun and of red dwarfs (low mass white dwarfs).
Among the densest objects, second only to black holes; young ones may be pulsars.
